institutionName: Institut d'études politiques de Paris (Sciences Po)

questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose Paris because I like the city and I wanted to try to live in it for a longer time. I have family and friends living there, which also played an important role, and I had heard good things about Sciences Po.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I really enjoyed the exchange. I experienced so much in those 3,5 months and met a lot of people. Going on exchange has been something I wanted to do for a long time, and I think it gave me a lot and made me grow. The most difficult thing for me was to relax. Since the exchange was only 3,5 months, I always felt like I wanted to get the most out of it.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was not that difficult.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Not much, but I didn't need much assistance.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I don't really know, since I didn't participate in the introduction week. I guess most of the orientation and assistance was given there.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It is not that easy to find (affordable) housing in Paris.  

Sciences Po has a website for housing. The website is very confusing, but I would still recommend having a look at it since it seems to offer some good opportunities. 

I wanted to live in a shared flat with other young people, so I found my housing on the website "lacartedescolocs" which is mostly for shared flats. I can recommend it. I found a room in a great apartment in the 11th arrondissement with two really nice flatmates for 800 euros per month. 

The cheapest option is probably to apply for a room in "La Fondation Danoise" in "La Cité Internationale". I think the price is between 550 and 650 euros per month, and you live surrounded by a lot of other young people. The only minus is the location - it is a bit far from the center and not in an interesting neighborhood.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
You will probably have to spend some time finding housing. But most of the rooms/studios get available approximately one month (or less) before the renting, so you don't need to start looking four months ahead. 
It is expensive to live in Paris, and you should probably be ready to pay around 700-1000 euros per month for housing. But if you are not too picky about the area and the room, you can maybe find something cheaper.

Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: As far as I remember it takes some time, but it is doable.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I don't really remember.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: The class registration was very stressful. It works on the first come first served principle, so you need to be ready and prepared when the registration opens.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Before the registration, I definitely recommend writing a list of all the courses you are interested in (and 3-5 alternatives for each in case you don't get your first priorities). When the registration opens, make sure to register for your mandatory classes (if any) as the first ones, because they can be filled up in a few minutes. I didn't succeed in getting all the courses I wanted even though I was well-prepared and fast. If a course is full, you can try to refresh the website for some minutes, and if you are lucky there will be a free place later on.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The offer of courses is big and they have more specific/niche courses than at Copenhagen University, which I really appreciated.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
It depends on the specific course. In general, I think the courses at Sciences Po were less academic and theoretical and more focused on facts. In all of my courses, the teachers made sure to make a good introduction in order to give everyone the same base. 
During the semester you will have to prepare several presentations and do some assignments, but the amount of reading is less than at Copenhagen University, so I wouldn't say the workload was bigger at Sciences Po. At the end of the semester, there are fewer big exams than at KU, so for me, it felt more chill than at KU in general.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The style of teaching is very different from the one at Copenhagen University. You get more evaluated during the semester and there are fewer exams. In many of my classes, I had to do presentations and assignments during the semester and I only had a small Q&A at the end of the semester (and not a real exam). The system reminds me a bit of Danish high schools in that way. It is mandatory to attend the classes. I got the impression that there are fewer big lectures and more teaching in small classes of 20-30 people.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Comparative Politics (ASPO 25A11)
European Integration and its Challenges (DSPO 25A02)
Europe in the World Economy (DECO 25A03)
The Age of Economists (DECO 25A05)
L'économie au Défi du Genre (CECO 25F01)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I can recommend L'économie au Défi du Genre (CECO 25F01). That was definitely my favorite class. The teacher (Helene Perivier) is very good: She knows a lot about the subject, is very motivated, and has done some interesting work/papers. Be aware that it is in french.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: It was more expensive to go out than I thought. Especially if you want to go to nightclubs, many of them cost around 20 euros for the entrance. But you can definitely find a lot of cheaper (and less known) and great places to go out!

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
More expensive than expected: clubs, drinks/beers at bars, public transportation, supermarkets.
Less expensive than expected: books (for most of the classes, you don't need to buy any books), bike rental, the cafeteria at Sciences Po:-)

If you get around by public transportation it can be worth it to buy a Navigo pass. But If you don't want to spend 80 euros per month on transportation, I would recommend registering for a Velib pass. You pay either 3,10 euros per month (for only non-electric bikes) or 8,30 euros per month (including electric bikes) for unlimited use of bikes (and there are a lot of stations all around the city). That is what I did, and I really enjoyed biking around the city, which is also often faster than taking the metro.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were a lot of activities available at Sciences Po. They have a lot of associations, and they also offer many sport activities for a cheap price. If you want to register for a sport activity, you need to keep updated on when the registration opens and to be ready to register when it opens, since the activities get booked very fast.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I didn't register for any of the activities at Sciences Po, but I heard that many of the sports were great and also the cinema association.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Museums! Paris has a lot of amazing museums, and if you are under 26, many of them are free! 
I personally like the north of Paris: the 9th, 10th, 11th, and 18th arrondissements are my favorite ones: A lot of bars and places to go out, and cheaper than the arrondissements around Sciences Po.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was pretty easy. Sciences Po is a very international school with a lot of other exchange students, so you don't feel like you have to adapt to a specific french culture at school.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Try to do some of the group work with french people from your class - that's how I made french friends at Sciences Po. 
Else, I think being part of an association or doing a sport at Sciences Po is a good way to meet local students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I didn't find many cultural differences.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
The late lifestyle. The French people I met and lived with had another rhythm than many Danes. Fx eating lunch and dinner way later than in Denmark. 

The food seems more important in France. People gather more for dinner or lunch, and it is easy to find good and cheap food in many places.

The nightlife. First, I was a bit disappointed about the clubs (and the expensive entrance). But there are so many smaller clubs/bars that have events and concerts almost every night. Also, people, in general, seem to get less drunk than in Denmark when going out, and I appreciated getting used to going out without being completely wasted.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Try to find a balance between studying and exploring/enjoying the city and life in Paris. 

Don't stress too much about meeting people in the beginning. You can easily meet new people after the first weeks as well, so remember to take a rest sometimes. 

Even though it at first can seem expensive to go out, that shouldn't hold you back. You can find a lot of cheaper places if you search a bit (especially in the north of Paris).

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be prepared for another way of teaching and evaluating students. In the beginning, it might be a bit overwhelming to have to do so many presentations, but remember that on the other hand, you will have fewer big exams and less reading.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
The people I met and the relationships I got. 
Also, it was the first time I lived abroad on my own, and I learned a lot about myself from this experience. I think it made me more open and confident in general.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: For me, the biggest challenge was my FOMO. There were always people wanting to go out, and in Paris, there is always a nice event you can attend. Since I was only there for a short time, I felt like I didn't want to miss anything. Next time I would be more aware of taking time to relax.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
